pronunciation.title: The 3 sound rules that unlock French
points: Final consonants go silent: the s, t, d, p, x at the end of most words are not pronounced — 'salut' is 'sah-loo', 'beaucoup' is 'boku'.
'on', 'an', 'en', 'in', 'ain' are ONE nasal sound each: push air through your nose and never fully say the n — 'bon' [bɔ̃], 'vin' [vɛ̃].
The French R lives in the throat — a soft gargle, as in 'merci' and 'rue'. And the letter h is always silent: 'heure' starts with a vowel sound.

grammar.title: How French spelling maps to sound
grammar.explanation: French spelling looks scary but it is very regular — more regular than English. Three rules unlock almost everything: (1) final consonants (s, t, d, p, x) are usually silent; (2) 'on', 'an', 'en', 'in', 'ain' are single nasal vowels, and the n is never fully pronounced; (3) the French R is made at the back of the throat, like a soft gargle, never rolled. Learn these and you can read any French word out loud.

pronunciation.title: Sound natural: liaisons and the u / ou trap
points: Liaison: when a word ending in a silent consonant meets a vowel, the consonant wakes up and links — 'vous‿avez' sounds like 'voo-zah-vay', 'les‿amis' like 'lay-zah-mee'.
'u' [y] and 'ou' [u] are different sounds: 'tu' (you) vs 'tout' (all). Round your lips tight and push the sound forward for 'u'.
Yes/no questions rise at the end: 'Tu vas bien ?' goes UP. In listening exams, that rising tune signals a question even with no question word.

grammar.title: Tu vs vous — the two words for 'you'
grammar.explanation: French has two words for 'you'. Use 'tu' with friends, family, children and people your age; use 'vous' with strangers, older people, shops and officials. The verb changes too: 'tu parles' but 'vous parlez'. When in doubt, 'vous' is always safe — nobody is ever offended by too much politeness.

pronunciation.title: É vs è, and verbs that lose their endings
points: 'é' [e] is bright and closed ('café', 'répétez'); 'è' [ɛ] is open ('m'appelle' [mapɛl], 'mère'). Mixing them is the number-one beginner giveaway.
Verb endings in -ent are silent: 'ils parlent' sounds exactly like 'il parle' [paʁl]. Only the pronoun tells you singular or plural.
'Je' shrinks before a vowel: je + appelle = 'j'appelle' [ʒapɛl]. Never say 'je appelle'.

grammar.title: S'appeler and être (je / tu / il / vous)
grammar.explanation: Two verbs introduce you to the world. 'S'appeler' (to call oneself) gives your name: je m'appelle, tu t'appelles, il s'appelle, vous vous appelez. 'Être' (to be) gives everything else: je suis, tu es, il est, vous êtes. Notice the pattern: the little word before the verb (me / te / se / vous) always matches who you are talking about.

pronunciation.title: Numbers are a pronunciation workout
points: 'x' is silent in 'deux' [dø], 'six' [sis], 'dix' [dis] — but it buzzes as [z] in 'dix-sept' [dizsɛt] and 'dix-neuf'.
Nasal vowels carry the tens: 'trente' [tʁɑ̃t], 'cent' [sɑ̃], 'vingt' [vɛ̃]. Keep the air in your nose.
Stress the LAST syllable: soixante-DIX, quatre-VINGTS. Flat English stress makes numbers hard to catch.

grammar.title: Building numbers: the rules (and the weird 70–99)
grammar.explanation: After 16, French builds numbers with logic — except 70 to 99, which are famously weird. 17–19 are 'ten-seven' (dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf). 20–69 combine tens and ones (trente-quatre), with 'et' only in 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 (vingt et un). Then: 70 = sixty-ten (soixante-dix), 80 = four-twenties (quatre-vingts), 90 = four-twenty-ten (quatre-vingt-dix). Examiners love testing these — drill them until they're automatic.

pronunciation.title: Family words are full of è and silent letters
points: 'père, mère, frère' all use the open è [ɛ] — don't say 'may-re', say [mɛʁ].

grammar.title: Mon / ma / mes — possessives
grammar.explanation: Possessives agree with the thing owned, not the owner: 'mon père' (my father — masculine), 'ma mère' (my mother — feminine), 'mes parents' (my parents — plural). One famous exception: a feminine word starting with a vowel or silent h takes 'mon' for smooth sound — 'mon amie' (my female friend), never 'ma amie'.

pronunciation.title: The great vowel combos: eau, ai, oi
points: 'eau' is always [o]: l'eau [lo], gâteau [gato]. Three letters, one sound.
'ai' is [ɛ]: lait [lɛ], aimer [eme], viande [vjɑ̃d]. Don't say 'lay'.
'oi' is [wa]: poisson [pwasɔ̃], boire [bwaʁ]. And g + e/i = [ʒ]: fromage [fʁɔmaʒ], manger [mɑ̃ʒe].

grammar.title: Du / de la / de l' / des — the partitive articles
grammar.explanation: When you mean 'some' of something, French needs a partitive article: 'du' for masculine (du pain), 'de la' for feminine (de la viande), 'de l'' before a vowel (de l'eau), 'des' for plural. But after a negation, they all collapse to 'de': 'Je mange du pain' becomes 'Je ne mange pas de pain'. For general likes and dislikes, use le/la instead: 'J'aime le fromage' (cheese in general).

pronunciation.title: Polite sounds: eu, and softening your requests
points: 'eu' in 'serveur' is [œ] — relaxed, like 'uh': [sɛʁvœʁ]. Don't say 'serve-oor'.
'je voudrais' [ʒə vudʁɛ] ends open and soft — that gentle [ɛ] ending is exactly what makes it polite.
'ch' is always [ʃ]: cher [ʃɛʁ]. And 'th' is just [t]: thé [te] — never the English 'th'.

grammar.title: Vouloir / pouvoir + the magic 'je voudrais'
grammar.explanation: 'Vouloir' (to want): je veux, tu veux, vous voulez. 'Pouvoir' (can, to be able to): je peux, tu peux, vous pouvez. At a café, never bark 'je veux' at a stranger — use the conditional 'je voudrais' (I would like), the magic politeness word. 'Tu peux' is for friends; 'vous pouvez' opens every polite request to strangers.

pronunciation.title: Time words: silent h and tricky vowels
points: 'h' is always silent: 'heure' [œʁ], 'hier' [jɛʁ], 'huit' [ɥit]. 'L'heure' flows as one sound: [lœʁ].
'aujourd'hui' is [oʒuʁdɥi] — say it in two beats, 'o-zhoor-dwee': practice slowly, then speed up.
'en' = [ɑ̃]: 'en juillet' [ɑ̃ ʒɥijɛ]. And 'mercredi' — every letter counts, don't swallow the middle.

grammar.title: Il est + time; days and months
grammar.explanation: 'Il est' + number + 'heure(s)' tells the time: 'Il est trois heures.' Halves and quarters: 'et demie' (half past), 'et quart' (quarter past), 'moins le quart' (quarter to). Days of the week take no article for a specific day: 'Nous sommes lundi' — with 'le' it would mean 'on Mondays'. Months follow 'en': 'en juillet', 'en décembre'. The months: janvier, février, mars, avril, mai, juin, juillet, août, septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre. The seasons: le printemps, l'été, l'automne, l'hiver.

units.title: Être and Avoir
objectives: Conjugate 'être' and 'avoir' fully in the present tense

'é / ée' endings are bright [e]: fatigué [fatige], mariée [maʁje]. Keep them short and crisp.
'âge' has a soft g: [aʒ], like the 's' in English 'measure'.

grammar.title: Être and avoir — full present tense
grammar.explanation: The two pillars of French. Être (to be): je suis, tu es, il/elle est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils/elles sont. Avoir (to have): j'ai, tu as, il/elle a, nous avons, vous avez, ils/elles ont. French uses 'avoir' where English uses 'to be' for age, hunger, thirst and temperature: 'J'ai 30 ans', 'J'ai faim', 'Il a froid'. Say both tables out loud every day until they're automatic.

points: 'gare' [gaʁ] (station) vs 'garde' [gaʁd] (guard): that final d IS pronounced in 'garde'. One consonant changes the word.

Cities simply take 'à': à Paris, à Toronto.

vocab.tip: Pronounced like 'ee-air' — the h is silent.

pronunciation.title: The silent endings of the past
points: Past participles in -é sound like 'ay': regardé = ruh-gar-DAY. Never pronounce the final consonant that isn't there.
In 'ils ont fini', the t of 'ont' is silent: eel zon fee-NEE. Link it smoothly, don't pop the t.
J'ai is one single sound: 'zhay'. Don't say jeh-ah-ee — melt it together.

grammar.title: Passé composé with avoir: j'ai + past participle
grammar.explanation: To talk about a finished action in the past, use the present of avoir plus the past participle: j'ai mangé (I ate / I have eaten). Regular verbs: -er becomes -é (parler → parlé), -ir becomes -i (finir → fini), -re becomes -u (vendre → vendu). Memorize the irregulars — the exam loves them: faire → fait, prendre → pris, voir → vu, dire → dit, écrire → écrit.

points: The extra -e and -s of agreement are almost always SILENT: allé, allée, allés, allées all sound identical. Spelling carries the meaning.

With être, the past participle AGREES with the subject: add -e for feminine, -s for plural. Il est allé, elle est allée, ils sont allés, elles sont allées.

points: Je parlais, tu parlais, il parlait, ils parlaient are pronounced IDENTICALLY: par-LAY. Only spelling shows the difference — a favorite dictation trap.
The plural forms stand out: nous parlions (par-lee-ON), vous parliez (par-lee-AY). Hear the 'ee' glide.
Être is the one rebel: j'étais, tu étais — the stem is ét-, not es-.

grammar.title: Imparfait: 'nous' stem + endings — vs passé composé

pronunciation.title: Future endings: the R you must pronounce
points: The futur simple has a hard, pronounced R: je parlerai = par-luh-RAY. Don't swallow it.
'Je vais parler' (near future) vs 'je parlerai' (simple future): the first has two separate words, the second is one word ending in -ai. The exam will test your ear on this.

grammar.title: Futur proche vs futur simple
grammar.explanation: Futur proche = present of aller + infinitive (je vais manger) — for soon, certain plans. Futur simple = infinitive + -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont (je parlerai) — for later or less certain events. For -re verbs, drop the final e: prendre → prendrai. Memorize the irregular stems: être → ser-, avoir → aur-, aller → ir-, faire → fer-, venir → viendr-, vouloir → voudr-, pouvoir → pourr-.

quiz.q: Which sentence is futur proche?
quiz.explain: Aller + infinitive = futur proche: je vais manger.

quiz.explain: Futur simple of partir: nous partirons. 'Allons partir' is futur proche — read the instruction!

units.title: Les pronoms
objectives: Replace nouns with le, la, les (direct) and lui, leur (indirect).
Place pronouns BEFORE the verb — including before the auxiliary in passé composé.
Meet y and en: j'y vais, j'en veux.
units.imagePrompt: flat vector illustration of speech bubbles with arrows replacing nouns with the pronouns le la les lui leur

vocab.tip: Takes à → use lui/leur: je lui téléphone.
No preposition in French: j'attends Marie.
Je connais, tu connais, il connaît.

phrases.en: I see him / I see it.
I am talking to him / to her.

pronunciation.title: Liaisons and contractions with pronouns
points: Before a vowel, le/la become l': je l'ai vu, elle l'aime. One smooth sound — never 'je le ai'.
Les + vowel makes a liaison: les‿amis = lay-zah-MEE. That z is mandatory.
Don't confuse leur (to them, pronoun) with leurs (their, possessive plural): je leur parle vs leurs amis.

grammar.title: Object pronouns go BEFORE the verb
grammar.explanation: Direct objects (le, la, les = him/her/it/them) and indirect objects (lui, leur = to him/her, to them) go directly BEFORE the verb: je le vois, je lui parle. In the passé composé, the pronoun jumps before the auxiliary: je l'ai vu. Exam bonus: with avoir, the participle agrees with a preceding DIRECT object — je les ai vus. Light intro: y replaces à + place (j'y vais = I'm going there), en replaces de + thing (j'en veux = I want some).

examples.fr: Je le regarde chaque jour.
examples.en: I watch it every day.

examples.fr: Elle lui a téléphoné hier.
examples.en: She called him yesterday. / She called her yesterday.

examples.fr: Je les ai vus hier.
examples.en: I saw them yesterday. (agreement with preceding les)

examples.fr: Tu y vas demain ?
examples.en: Are you going there tomorrow?

units.title: Au travail
objectives: Talk about professions, the office, and your daily routine.
Conjugate reflexive verbs: je me lève, tu te lèves, ils se lèvent.
Use reflexives in the passé composé with être — and make them agree.

vocab.tip: Une patronne for a female boss.

pronunciation.title: The dropped E in reflexive pronouns
points: Me, te, se are soft and quick: 'je me lève' = zhuh muh lev. Don't stress the pronoun.
Before a vowel, se becomes s': elle s'habille, il s'appelle. Glide it together.
In 'nous nous levons', pronounce BOTH 'nous' clearly — beginners swallow the second one.

grammar.title: Reflexive verbs: je me lève, tu te lèves…
grammar.explanation: Reflexive verbs add a pronoun before the verb: me, te, se, nous, vous, se. Je me lève, tu te lèves, il/elle se lève, nous nous levons, vous vous levez, ils/elles se lèvent. In the passé composé they ALWAYS use être: je me suis levé(e) — and the participle agrees with the subject, just like other être verbs.

units.title: Les voyages
objectives: Use en/à correctly with transport: en train, à pied.
Book a hotel room and navigate the airport.
Ask questions three ways: intonation, est-ce que, inversion (TEF speaking A).
units.imagePrompt: flat vector illustration of a suitcase, a train, an airplane and a small hotel building with question marks above them

vocab.tip: Literally 'by foot' — uses à, not en!

phrases.fr: Il va à l'aéroport en bus.
phrases.en: He is going to the airport by bus.

phrases.fr: Nous allons à l'hôtel à pied.
phrases.en: We are walking to the hotel.

phrases.fr: Où est l'aéroport, s'il vous plaît ?
Est-ce que vous avez une chambre ?
À quelle heure part le train ?
phrases.en: At what time does the train leave?

pronunciation.title: Question music: rising intonation
points: Yes/no questions in speech simply RISE at the end: 'Vous venez demain↗?' The music does the work of the question mark.
'Est-ce que' melts into one chunk: ess-kuh. Say 'Est-ce que tu viens ?' fast and it becomes 'ess-kuh too vee-AN'.
In inversion, the -t- is pronounced and links: 'Partez-vous ?' = par-tay VOO — hear that t clearly.

grammar.title: En/à with transport + three ways to ask
grammar.explanation: Use EN for vehicles you ride inside: en train, en avion, en bus, en voiture. Use À for open transport or your own feet: à pied, à vélo, à moto. Three ways to ask a question: (1) raise your voice — 'Tu viens ?'; (2) add 'est-ce que' — 'Est-ce que tu viens ?'; (3) invert verb and subject — 'Viens-tu ?' For TEF speaking, (1) and (2) are plenty; inversion is formal and mostly written.

examples.fr: Je vais à Paris en avion.
examples.en: I'm going to Paris by plane.

examples.fr: Elle voyage à pied.
examples.en: She travels on foot.

examples.fr: Est-ce que tu as réservé une chambre ?
examples.en: Did you book a room?

examples.fr: Partez-vous demain ?
examples.en: Are you leaving tomorrow? (formal inversion)

quiz.explain: Vehicles you ride inside take en: en train, en avion, en bus.

quiz.explain: À pied — on foot always uses à. The classic exception to en!

quiz.q: Which question uses inversion?
quiz.explain: Inversion swaps verb and subject with a hyphen: Partez-vous ?

quiz.q: Choose: ___ vous avez une chambre ?
quiz.explain: Est-ce que turns a statement into a yes/no question: Est-ce que vous avez une chambre ?

quiz.q: Listen and choose the correct meaning.
quiz.explain: Est-ce que vous avez réservé — passé composé of réserver: Did you book?

quiz.q: Listen and choose the correct meaning.

units.title: La santé
objectives: Name body parts and describe symptoms: j'ai mal à la tête.
See a doctor in French: explain what's wrong, understand advice.
Use devoir, pouvoir, vouloir + il faut + infinitive correctly.
units.imagePrompt: flat vector illustration of a friendly doctor talking to a patient, with labeled body parts around them

vocab.tip: J'ai mal à la tête = I have a headache.
Silent h, and the ô wears a circumflex.

phrases.en: One must rest. / You need to rest.

pronunciation.title: The silent letters in body parts
points: Le dos: the final s is completely silent — just say 'doh'. Same for le bras: 'brah'.
Le cœur: the œ ligature is ONE vowel sound, like the 'u' in 'burn': kuhr.
L'hôpital: the h is silent (loh-pee-TAL), and the circumflex on ô is a hint that an old s disappeared.

grammar.title: Devoir, pouvoir, vouloir + il faut + infinitive
grammar.explanation: These three modal verbs are followed DIRECTLY by an infinitive — no preposition: je dois partir (I must leave), tu peux venir (you can come), elle veut manger (she wants to eat). They're irregular: je dois / tu dois / il doit / nous devons; je peux / tu peux / il peut / nous pouvons; je veux / tu veux / il veut / nous voulons / vous voulez / ils veulent. 'Il faut + infinitive' means 'it's necessary to': il faut travailler.

examples.fr: Je dois voir un médecin.
examples.en: I must see a doctor.

examples.fr: Tu peux attendre ici.
examples.en: You can wait here.

examples.fr: Elle veut se reposer.
examples.en: She wants to rest.

examples.fr: Il faut travailler.
examples.en: One has to work. / It's necessary to work.

quiz.explain: Devoir with je: je dois. Then the infinitive directly: je dois partir.

quiz.explain: Pouvoir with tu: tu peux. Tu peux venir demain.

quiz.explain: Il faut is followed directly by the infinitive — no preposition: il faut travailler.

quiz.explain: Vouloir with elle: elle veut. Elle veut se reposer.

quiz.explain: Avoir mal à la tête = to have a headache.

quiz.q: Listen and choose the correct meaning.
quiz.explain: Vous devez = you must (devoir). Vous devez vous reposer: You must rest.

units.title: Donner son avis
objectives: Give opinions: à mon avis, je pense que, selon moi.
Justify with parce que + sentence and pour + infinitive.
Structure a TEF speaking section B answer: opinion + reason + example.
units.imagePrompt: flat vector illustration of two people having a polite debate, speech bubbles showing à mon avis and parce que

vocab.tip: À mon avis = in my opinion.
Je pense que = I think that.
Je trouve ça bien = I think it's good.
Je ne suis pas d'accord = I disagree.

phrases.en: In my view, one must work.

pronunciation.title: Sounding convinced, not robotic
points: In 'je pense que', the 'que' is a soft, quick 'kuh' — don't punch it: zhuh ponss-kuh.
'Parce que' runs together into two beats: parss-kuh. Native speakers never separate it.
'D'accord' links the d': dah-KOR. That little apostrophe is a bridge, not a wall.

grammar.title: Opinion + justification: parce que / pour + infinitive
grammar.explanation: Give your opinion with 'à mon avis', 'je pense que', or 'selon moi'. Then ALWAYS justify it — an unjustified opinion scores nothing on the TEF. Use 'parce que + sentence' (because) or 'pour + infinitive' (in order to). The winning structure for TEF speaking section B is: opinion + reason + example.

examples.fr: À mon avis, le français est important parce que je veux travailler au Canada.
examples.en: In my opinion, French is important because I want to work in Canada.

examples.fr: Je pense que tu as raison.
examples.en: I think you're right.

examples.fr: Selon moi, il faut parler français pour trouver un travail.
examples.en: In my view, one must speak French to find a job.

examples.fr: Je suis d'accord avec toi parce que tu as raison.
examples.en: I agree with you because you're right.

lines.speaker: B

lines.en: Because it's important for finding a job.

lines.speaker: B

lines.en: Me, I think it's difficult.

lines.speaker: A

lines.en: Why is it important?

lines.fr: Parce que je veux travailler au Canada et parler avec mes collègues.
lines.en: Because I want to work in Canada and talk with my colleagues.

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: You're right!

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: So, shall we speak French together?

lines.speaker: B
lines.fr: D'accord ! Je suis d'accord avec toi !
lines.en: Agreed! I agree with you!

quiz.explain: 'Pour + infinitive' expresses purpose: pour réussir = in order to succeed. 'Parce que' needs a full sentence after it.

quiz.q: What is the BEST structure for TEF speaking section B?
quiz.explain: Section B asks you to convince someone. Opinion alone scores little — always add parce que/pour and an example.

quiz.q: Complete: Je pense ___ tu as raison.
quiz.explain: Je pense QUE + sentence. No preposition between them.

quiz.q: Complete: ___ moi, c'est important.
quiz.explain: Selon moi = in my view. (À mon avis is the other fixed form — never 'à mon moi'.)

I think it's important to visit Canada.
I want to work because Canada is important.
quiz.explain: À mon avis (opinion) + parce que (reason): In my opinion it's important because I want to work in Canada.

quiz.q: Listen and choose the correct meaning.
quiz.explain: Je suis d'accord avec toi = I agree with you. The TEF loves testing this against 'pas d'accord'.

units.title: Raconter une histoire
objectives: Order events with connectors: d'abord, ensuite, puis, soudain, enfin.
Combine imparfait (background) + passé composé (events) to narrate.
Tell a complete anecdote — the core skill for TEF writing and speaking.
units.imagePrompt: flat vector illustration of an open storybook with connected panels showing sun, rain and a traveler

vocab.tip: L'histoire se termine bien = The story ends well.

phrases.fr: Soudain, nous avons vu un ami.
Tout à coup, il a neigé.
phrases.en: All of a sudden, it snowed.

pronunciation.title: Storytelling rhythm
points: Pause AFTER connectors: 'D'abord… [beat] il faisait beau.' That pause is what makes you sound like a storyteller, not a robot.
Soudain: stress the LAST syllable — soo-DAN. French stress is almost always final.
Ensuite flows as one word: 'on-sweet'. Don't chop it into en-suite.

grammar.title: Narrating: imparfait for background, passé composé for events
grammar.explanation: A story needs BOTH past tenses. The imparfait paints the background — the weather, what people were doing: il faisait beau, nous marchions. The passé composé moves the story forward — the events: soudain, il a plu. Connectors order everything: d'abord → ensuite / puis → soudain → enfin. This combination is exactly what TEF writing and speaking reward.

examples.fr: D'abord, il faisait beau et nous étions en ville.
examples.en: First, the weather was nice and we were downtown.

examples.fr: Ensuite, nous sommes partis.
examples.en: Then, we left.

examples.fr: Soudain, il a plu et nous sommes rentrés.
examples.en: Suddenly, it rained and we went home.

examples.fr: Enfin, nous avons mangé ensemble à la maison.
examples.en: Finally, we ate together at home.

quiz.q: Which connector STARTS a story?
quiz.explain: D'abord opens the narration. Enfin closes it; soudain/tout à coup mark surprises in the middle.

vocab.tip: One épreuve = one of the four parts of the test
Always read la consigne before you start
Plan on le brouillon before your final text
TEF loves les pièges — answers that sound right but aren't

pronunciation.title: Exam-day tips: listening & speaking
points: In compréhension orale you hear each recording exactly ONCE — be focused from the first second.
In expression orale, speak loudly and clearly into the recorder. Mumbling costs you points.
If you stumble while speaking, keep going. Never stop and restart a sentence.

grammar.title: How TEF Canada is scored
grammar.explanation: The test has four independent sections, each with its own score. Listening and reading are machine-scored multiple-choice tests. Speaking and writing are each marked independently by two trained examiners. Your scores are converted to CLB / NCLC levels — the scale Canada's immigration system uses. For Express Entry, the key threshold is CLB 7 in EVERY section: that is what unlocks up to 50 bonus CRS points for French.

examples.fr: J'ai obtenu 260 en compréhension orale.
examples.en: I scored 260 in listening.

examples.fr: Il faut le niveau NCLC 7 dans les quatre épreuves.
examples.en: You need NCLC level 7 in all four test sections.

examples.fr: Les résultats sont valables deux ans.
examples.en: The results are valid for two years.

quiz.q: What is the widely-published TEF Canada score range for CLB 7 in compréhension écrite (reading)?
quiz.explain: Reading CLB 7 ≈ 207–232. Listening is 249–279; speaking and writing are 310–348. Always confirm current equivalences with your test center.

quiz.q: For Express Entry, what does reaching NCLC 7 in all four French abilities give you?
quiz.explain: Strong French (NCLC 7+ in all four abilities) adds up to 50 CRS points: 25 base, plus 25 more if your English is also CLB 5 or higher.

quiz.q: In the listening section, how many times do you hear each recording?
choices: As many times as you want

quiz.q: Is there a penalty for wrong answers in the listening and reading sections?

quiz.q: How long are TEF Canada results valid for immigration?
quiz.explain: Two years from the test date — plan your Express Entry profile timing accordingly.

units.title: Listening: beat the traps
objectives: Read the questions and answers BEFORE the audio starts
Spot the classic traps: numbers, dates, and negatives
Take quick notes on key facts while listening
units.imagePrompt: flat vector illustration of oversized headphones above a speech bubble with sound waves and a question mark, listening test concept, clean minimal style, blue accents

vocab.en: for lack of / due to a lack of

pronunciation.title: Listening strategy: before, during, after
points: BEFORE the audio: read the question and all four answers. Underline key words — numbers, dates, names.
DURING: take short notes, especially numbers, days, and anything negative (pas, jamais, ne... plus).
AFTER: eliminate answers that contradict what you heard. If unsure, guess — there is no penalty.

grammar.title: The distractor trap
grammar.explanation: Wrong answers in TEF listening are not random — they are built to trap you. One classic trap repeats a word from the recording but changes its meaning. Another gives the right information with the wrong number or date. A third states the opposite of what was said, hoping you missed a negative like 'ne... plus'. Your defense: match the MEANING, not the words.

quiz.q: From which platform does the 8:47 train to Québec leave?
quiz.transcript: Attention, voyageurs : le train de 8 h 47 à destination de Québec partira du quai numéro 5, et non du quai numéro 3 comme annoncé précédemment.
quiz.explain: Trap: 'quai numéro 3' is mentioned — but only to correct it. The train leaves from platform 5.

quiz.q: When is the museum open on July 14?
quiz.transcript: Le musée sera fermé le lundi, comme d'habitude, mais il ouvrira exceptionnellement ce lundi 14 juillet de 10 h à 18 h.
quiz.explain: Trap: 'fermé le lundi' — but this Monday is an exception. Listen for 'exceptionnellement'.

quiz.q: Will the woman go to the party?
quiz.transcript: — Tu viens à la fête samedi ? — J'aimerais bien, mais je travaille jusqu'à 22 h. — Pas de problème, on commence à 21 h mais ça finit tard !
quiz.explain: She works until 10 p.m., but the party 'finit tard' (ends late) — so she can come after work.

quiz.q: Why are the Toronto flights cancelled?
quiz.transcript: En raison d'une grève, les vols à destination de Toronto sont annulés aujourd'hui. Les passagers sont priés de contacter la compagnie.
quiz.explain: 'En raison d'une grève' = due to a strike. Don't invent other reasons.

quiz.q: What is the monthly rent?
quiz.transcript: — L'appartement fait combien de mètres carrés ? — Quatre-vingt-dix. — Et le loyer ? — Mille deux cents dollars par mois, charges comprises.
quiz.explain: Number trap: 90 (quatre-vingt-dix) is the size in m², not the price. 'Charges comprises' = charges included.

quiz.q: When is the duty pharmacy open on Sunday?
quiz.transcript: La pharmacie de garde ce week-end est la pharmacie Centrale, rue Sainte-Catherine. Elle est ouverte samedi de 9 h à 20 h et dimanche de 10 h à 18 h.
quiz.explain: Trap: Saturday's hours (9 a.m.–8 p.m.) are stated first. Sunday is 10 a.m.–6 p.m.

units.title: Reading: speed and precision
objectives: Skim for structure before reading in detail
Answer chronology and inference questions
Manage 60 minutes across 50 questions without getting stuck
units.imagePrompt: flat vector illustration of an open newspaper with a magnifying glass over lines of text, reading test concept, clean minimal style, green accents

vocab.tip: In questions, 'sauf' reverses the whole logic!

phrases.fr: Contrairement à ce qui est dit,

pronunciation.title: Exam tips: reading
points: Read the QUESTIONS first, then skim the text for the answers — don't translate every word.
Watch for 'sauf', 'à l'exception de' in questions: they reverse the logic of the question.
For chronology questions, circle every date and time marker as you read.

grammar.title: Reading for inference — practice text 1
grammar.explanation: Some questions ask what is directly stated; others ask what you can INFER — what the text suggests without saying it outright. Inference answers are never wild guesses: they combine two or three clues from the text. And beware of absolutes: if an answer choice says 'toujours' (always) or 'jamais' (never), be suspicious — texts rarely support them. Read the text below, then answer the quiz.

examples.fr: À Montréal, le vélo-partage connaît un succès grandissant. Selon un sondage publié hier, plus de 60 % des utilisateurs prennent un vélo au moins trois fois par semaine.
examples.en: In Montréal, bike-sharing is enjoying growing success. According to a survey published yesterday, more than 60% of users take a bike at least three times a week.

examples.fr: Toutefois, le service fait face à un enjeu de taille : en hiver, le nombre d'utilisateurs chute de 80 %. La ville réfléchit donc à des vélos adaptés au froid.
examples.en: However, the service faces a major challenge: in winter, the number of users drops by 80%. The city is therefore considering bikes adapted to the cold.

examples.fr: « Nous voulons que le vélo reste une option toute l'année », souligne la mairesse. Un projet pilote sera lancé en janvier dans trois quartiers.
examples.en: 'We want cycling to remain an option all year round,' the mayor emphasizes. A pilot project will be launched in January in three neighbourhoods.

examples.fr: À l'instar de plusieurs villes européennes, Montréal espère ainsi réduire la circulation automobile de 15 % d'ici 2030.
examples.en: Following the example of several European cities, Montréal hopes to reduce car traffic by 15% by 2030.

lines.speaker: A

lines.en: The Verdun youth centre is offering new activities for the fall.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: Au programme : un atelier de cuisine les mardis soirs, un club de lecture les jeudis, et des sorties en plein air un samedi par mois.
lines.en: On the program: a cooking workshop on Tuesday evenings, a reading club on Thursdays, and outdoor outings one Saturday a month.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: Les inscriptions sont ouvertes jusqu'au 30 septembre. Attention : les places sont limitées à vingt participants par activité.
lines.en: Registration is open until September 30. Note: places are limited to twenty participants per activity.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: Contrairement à l'an dernier, toutes les activités seront gratuites cette année grâce à une subvention de la ville.
lines.en: Unlike last year, all activities will be free this year thanks to a city grant.

quiz.q: Text 1: how often do most bike-share users ride?
quiz.explain: 'au moins trois fois par semaine' — at least three times a week.

quiz.q: Text 1: what is the main challenge ('enjeu') mentioned?
choices: The 80% drop in users in winter
quiz.explain: The text names exactly one enjeu: winter use falls by 80%.

quiz.q: Text 1: what can be deduced about the mayor's position?
choices: She supports cycling all year round
She wants to close the service in winter
quiz.explain: 'Nous voulons que le vélo reste une option toute l'année' — she is clearly in favour.

quiz.q: Text 2: how often are the outdoor outings?
quiz.explain: 'un samedi par mois' — one Saturday per month.

quiz.q: Text 2: what is NEW this year at the youth centre?
quiz.explain: 'Contrairement à l'an dernier, toutes les activités seront gratuites' — free access is the change.

quiz.q: Text 2: which activity takes place on Tuesdays?
choices: None — the centre is closed on Tuesdays
quiz.explain: 'un atelier de cuisine les mardis soirs'.

units.title: Speaking: convince them
objectives: Section A: ask open, polite questions to get information (5 min)
Section B: deliver a structured persuasive speech — opinion, arguments, example, conclusion (10 min)
Use 10+ connectors naturally while speaking
units.imagePrompt: flat vector illustration of a confident person speaking into a microphone with speech bubbles and checkmarks, speaking test concept, clean minimal style, purple accents

phrases.en: On the one hand..., on the other hand...

phrases.fr: Il ne faut pas oublier que...

pronunciation.title: Speaking tips: exam day
points: Section A (5 min): ask as many questions as you can. Open questions (pourquoi, comment) earn more than yes/no ones.
Section B (10 min): keep talking for the full time. Silence is the only real failure.
Slow down and articulate. A calm, clear speaker scores higher than a fast, mumbling one.

grammar.title: The persuasion framework (Section B)
grammar.explanation: In Section B you must defend an opinion for several minutes. Use this framework every single time: 1) state your opinion clearly, 2) give TWO arguments, each introduced by a connector, 3) illustrate with a concrete example, 4) conclude by restating your opinion. Examiners reward structure as much as vocabulary — a well-organized B1 speech beats a chaotic B2 one.

examples.fr: À mon avis, le télétravail est une excellente chose.
examples.en: In my opinion, teleworking is an excellent thing.

examples.fr: D'une part, il fait gagner du temps ; d'autre part, il réduit le stress.
examples.en: On the one hand, it saves time; on the other hand, it reduces stress.

examples.fr: Prenons l'exemple de mon voisin : il a retrouvé deux heures par jour.
examples.en: Take my neighbour's example: he got back two hours a day.

examples.fr: C'est pourquoi je suis convaincu que le télétravail est l'avenir.
examples.en: That's why I'm convinced teleworking is the future.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: À mon avis, le télétravail devrait être proposé à tous les employés de bureau.
lines.en: In my opinion, teleworking should be offered to all office employees.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: D'une part, on évite les transports, qui sont fatigants et polluants. D'autre part, on est souvent plus concentré chez soi.
lines.en: On the one hand, you avoid commuting, which is tiring and polluting. On the other hand, you're often more focused at home.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: Prenons l'exemple de mon amie Julie : depuis qu'elle travaille à la maison, elle est moins stressée et plus efficace. Pour conclure, le télétravail est bon pour les employés et pour la planète.
lines.en: Take my friend Julie's example: since she started working from home, she's less stressed and more efficient. To conclude, teleworking is good for employees and for the planet.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: Selon moi, il faudrait interdire les voitures au centre-ville.
lines.en: In my view, cars should be banned from downtown.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: Tout d'abord, la pollution de l'air est dangereuse pour la santé. De plus, les rues seraient plus sûres pour les piétons et les cyclistes.
lines.en: First of all, air pollution is dangerous for health. Furthermore, streets would be safer for pedestrians and cyclists.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: À Montréal, certaines rues sont déjà piétonnes l'été, et les commerçants sont satisfaits. C'est pourquoi je pense que cette solution est l'avenir de nos villes.
lines.en: In Montréal, some streets are already pedestrian-only in summer, and shopkeepers are satisfied. That's why I think this solution is the future of our cities.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: Il me semble évident que les enfants devraient lire plus.
lines.en: It seems obvious to me that children should read more.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: D'une part, la lecture développe le vocabulaire et l'imagination. D'autre part, elle éloigne les enfants des écrans, au moins un moment.
lines.en: On the one hand, reading develops vocabulary and imagination. On the other hand, it keeps children away from screens, at least for a while.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: Par exemple, mon neveu lit vingt minutes chaque soir, et ses notes se sont améliorées. En conclusion, un livre par mois peut changer la vie d'un enfant.
lines.en: For example, my nephew reads twenty minutes every evening, and his grades have improved. In conclusion, one book a month can change a child's life.

quiz.q: Section A: you must get information about a language school. Which question is BEST?
choices: Pourriez-vous me dire quels cours vous proposez et à quels horaires ?
quiz.explain: Open + polite (conditionnel) beats closed yes/no questions — it forces a developed answer.

quiz.q: Which of these is a CLOSED question (avoid it in Section A)?
choices: Est-ce que l'école est ouverte le samedi ?
quiz.explain: Yes/no questions close the conversation. Prefer 'comment', 'pourquoi', 'quels'.

quiz.q: For Section B, which opening is strongest?
choices: À mon avis, les transports en commun devraient être gratuits.
Je ne sais pas quoi dire sur ce sujet.
Les transports en commun existent dans les villes.
quiz.explain: State a clear opinion immediately — the examiner needs a position to evaluate.

quiz.q: Which sentence makes the best ARGUMENT?
choices: D'une part, c'est moins cher ; d'autre part, c'est moins polluant.
quiz.explain: A real argument gives reasons, structured with connectors.

quiz.q: Which is the best concrete EXAMPLE?
choices: Prenons l'exemple de Lyon : depuis la gratuité, le nombre de voyageurs a augmenté de 30 %.
J'ai un exemple mais je l'ai oublié.
quiz.explain: Concrete and precise (a place, a number) = convincing.

quiz.q: Which conclusion works best?
choices: Pour conclure, je reste convaincu que la gratuité est une solution d'avenir.
Je n'ai plus rien à dire.
quiz.explain: Restate your opinion with a connector — never end with 'I have nothing more to say'.

units.titleFr: Expression écrite : des lettres qui rapportent

Section B: write a formal letter (200 words) with correct formules de politesse
Use 15 key connectors accurately and naturally

vocab.en: the subject line of a letter

vocab.tip: Friendly — for colleagues, NOT for formal complaints

phrases.en: On the one hand... on the other hand...

phrases.en: It is important to note that...

phrases.en: Please accept, Madam, Sir, the expression of my distinguished regards.

pronunciation.title: Exam tips: writing
points: Section A ≈ 80 words minimum (aim for ~100); Section B ≈ 200 words minimum. Count roughly as you write.
Keep 5 minutes at the end to re-read: check verb endings, agreements, and accents.
Never use 'tu' in Section B — a formal letter is always 'vous'.

grammar.title: Section A: the fait divers method
grammar.explanation: Section A asks for a short newspaper article (un fait divers) of about 80 words minimum. Method: answer four questions — QUI (who), QUOI (what), OÙ (where), QUAND (when) — then add one detail (a witness, a consequence, an investigation). Write in the passé composé, keep sentences short, and give your article a title. Below is a full model: read it, shadow the audio, then write your own on a different event.

examples.fr: INCENDIE DANS UN IMMEUBLE DU PLATEAU
examples.en: FIRE IN A PLATEAU APARTMENT BUILDING

examples.fr: Hier soir, vers 21 h, un incendie s'est déclaré dans un immeuble de trois étages de la rue Rachel, à Montréal.
examples.en: Last night, around 9 p.m., a fire broke out in a three-storey building on Rachel Street in Montréal.

examples.fr: Selon les témoins, les flammes sont parties d'une cuisine au deuxième étage. Les secours, arrivés rapidement, ont évacué douze personnes. Aucun blessé grave n'est à déplorer.
examples.en: According to witnesses, the flames started in a second-floor kitchen. Emergency services, arriving quickly, evacuated twelve people. No serious injuries are reported.

examples.fr: L'origine du sinistre reste inconnue. Une enquête est en cours.
examples.en: The cause of the fire remains unknown. An investigation is underway.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Subject: noise disturbance — request for action

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Dear Madam, Dear Sir,

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: Je me permets de vous écrire au sujet des travaux qui ont lieu dans l'immeuble depuis le 2 septembre.
lines.en: I am writing to you regarding the construction work taking place in the building since September 2.

lines.speaker: A
lines.fr: En effet, le bruit commence chaque jour à 6 h 30 du matin, ce qui m'empêche de dormir et de travailler. De plus, la poussière rend l'escalier difficile d'accès pour les personnes âgées.
lines.en: Indeed, the noise starts every day at 6:30 a.m., which prevents me from sleeping and working. Furthermore, the dust makes the stairwell difficult to access for elderly people.

lines.fr: C'est pourquoi je vous demande de bien vouloir faire respecter les horaires légaux, soit de 8 h à 18 h en semaine.
lines.en: That is why I ask you to please enforce the legal working hours, namely 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. on weekdays.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: Marie Tremblay, apartment 12

quiz.q: Complete the formal letter closing: « Je vous prie d'agréer, Madame, Monsieur, ... »
quiz.explain: The full formal formula is expected in Section B — memorize it exactly.

quiz.q: Which connector introduces a CONSEQUENCE?
quiz.explain: 'Par conséquent' = therefore. 'Cependant' = however (opposition); 'par exemple' = example.

quiz.q: In a formal complaint letter, which greeting is correct?
quiz.explain: Formal letters open with 'Madame, Monsieur,' — never casual greetings or 'tu' forms.

quiz.q: Choose the sentence with the correct formal 'vous' form:
choices: Je vous demande de bien vouloir intervenir.
quiz.explain: Section B is always 'vous'. 'Je vous demande de bien vouloir...' is the polite formal standard.

quiz.q: Which connector shows OPPOSITION?
quiz.explain: 'En revanche' = on the other hand. The others add information or give reasons.

quiz.q: Your fait divers is only 45 words. What should you do?
choices: Add a detail (a witness, a consequence) to reach about 80–100 words
Write the title in bigger letters
quiz.explain: Section A needs about 80 words minimum — add one concrete detail: a witness, a consequence, or the investigation.
